questions.stem: Your agent's response ends with `stop_reason: "tool_use"`. What should your application do next?

options.text: Return the response to the user; the model has finished.
Run the requested tool and send its output back as a tool_result block in a user message.
Resend the same request with a higher max_tokens value.
Wait for the model to execute the tool and send a follow-up response.

questions.explanation: `tool_use` means Claude is asking your code to run a tool. Your application executes it and returns a `tool_result` with the matching `tool_use_id`.

whyWrong.A: The model has not finished; it is waiting for tool output.
whyWrong.C: That would address a `max_tokens` stop, not a tool request.
whyWrong.D: The model never executes tools itself.

questions.mindset: Your code owns execution; the model owns decisions.

questions.stem: A research agent occasionally runs for hundreds of iterations and generates large bills. Which change most directly fixes this?

options.text: Add an instruction asking the model to be concise.
Switch to a smaller model.
Enforce a maximum iteration and token budget in the loop, then request a best-effort summary when it is reached.
Remove tools that return long outputs.

questions.explanation: Hard limits in your loop are deterministic. A graceful summary keeps partial work useful.

whyWrong.A: Prompt instructions are not a reliable stop mechanism.
whyWrong.B: A smaller model may loop just as long.
whyWrong.D: This removes capability without bounding the loop.

questions.mindset: Enforce limits in code, not in prompts.

questions.scenario: A support agent calls an order-lookup API that sometimes times out.
questions.stem: How should the timeout be handled so the agent can recover?

options.text: Return a tool_result with is_error set to true and a short description of the timeout.
Silently return an empty result.
Abort the conversation and show a generic error.
Retry the tool forever until it succeeds.

questions.explanation: Reporting the error lets Claude decide to retry, use another tool, or tell the user.

whyWrong.B: An empty result looks like 'no order found' and leads to wrong answers.
whyWrong.C: Gives up even though the model could recover.
whyWrong.D: Unbounded retries can hang the loop.

questions.mindset: Surface failures to the model so it can adapt.

questions.stem: An invoice pipeline always extracts fields, validates them, then writes to the ledger. Which architecture fits best?

options.text: An autonomous agent with all three steps as tools.
A prompt-chaining workflow with a validation gate between steps.
An orchestrator that spawns a subagent per field.
A single prompt that does all three steps at once.

questions.explanation: The steps are fixed and ordered, so a deterministic chain with gates is cheaper and easier to test.

whyWrong.A: Autonomy adds unpredictability when the path is already known.
whyWrong.C: Massive overhead for a simple extraction.
whyWrong.D: Skips the validation gate and is harder to debug.

questions.mindset: Use the simplest architecture that meets the requirement.

questions.stem: Which TWO situations most justify delegating to subagents?

options.text: Independent research subtasks that can run in parallel.
A task where every step needs the full shared state of the previous one.
Subtasks that each require reading many documents that would clutter the main context.
A single short classification request.

questions.explanation: Subagents help through parallelism and context isolation.

whyWrong.B: Tightly coupled steps suffer from the hand-off overhead.
whyWrong.D: A single call is simpler and cheaper.

questions.mindset: Delegate for isolation or parallelism, not for prestige.

questions.stem: An orchestrator's subagents return 20-page transcripts, and the orchestrator starts losing track of the goal. What is the best fix?

options.text: Ask subagents to return concise, structured summaries with only what the orchestrator needs.
Increase the orchestrator's max_tokens.
Merge all subagents into the orchestrator.
Run subagents sequentially instead of in parallel.

questions.explanation: Subagents protect the orchestrator's context only if they hand back compact results.

whyWrong.B: Output length is not the problem; input context is.
whyWrong.D: Ordering does not reduce what flows back.

questions.mindset: Design the hand-off contract between agents.
